speaker: George Lepard
words: As I say, one of the early day doctors, they had their own method of putting some medicines together and he had an account with a Spokane drug company in Spokane. When we were up at Melrose, I can remember the drugs were delivered by the stage line. Never had too much to come, just in small boxes. I do remember though that he had a very small showcase and that was always moved wherever we went and in that showcase would be different things that people would like but I know the top self always had chocolate candy and he would always have some chocolate candy himself and I have an idea that the young children got free samples. There's one thing about it, my father always had a team of horses and it wouldn't make any difference what time of day, night or how much anyone owed him if they called him to come if someone was sick we would bundle up regardless of the weather and take off and I can remember seeing him several times when he was dressed in real heavy clothing. He had a very special pork cap that he pulled down over his head and you could just barely see his eyes but that was one thing about it, my dad went when he was called.

speaker: George Lepard
words: Now when we moved to Potlatch in 1907, I went to Potlatch in 1907, my folks went in 1906. I stayed with my stepmother's folks in Moscow and the Potlatch Lumber Company was started in September… the 22nd in 1905. They burnt down a small shack, it was a log cabin, squadron shack they were called and I believe that is where the power plant for the Potlatch Mill is sitting today on the spot where this log cabin is located. In 1906 they started the mill and started an operation and the first manager was a fellow by the name of William Derry and he was appointed by the Weyerhaeuser company and the mill at the time it was built was built in Latah County about nine miles from Coos, Washington on the Potlatch River. The Weyerhaeuser company had heard about the big pine stand of timber that was in Latah County and they bought all that they could get a hold of. And they came to Latah County and there was a real nice meadow where they built the mill. Potlatch is a name from the Indian name and it means a great feast or general distribution of good things. Therefore they thought that Potlatch would be the logical name for the new mill.

speaker: George Lepard
words: Now the Washington, Idaho and Montana Railroad which might be called the Stump Dodger or the Washington Ironing and Mending Railroad was built between Coos, Washington and Bovill, Idaho. And although it's a separate organization from the Potlatch Company, it played a very important part in the development of the mill because it gave the outlet at both Coos to the Great Northern Pacific and the Inland Electric Train that was running at that time. And then there was a line built in from St. Mary's to Elk River that made connections at Bovill. And it gave a very good outlet for all of the lumber. The first two locomotives that run the passenger trains were number one and two and they had three coaches that I remember when they first started that ran to Palouse and then from Palouse to Bovill and then back to Palouse and then back to Potlatch. That was a day's work. And they sometimes had what they called a mix train. They didn't have enough to run a freight train. The engines number one and two, since it was down grade, they were capable of moving a 40-grid sized mix train which would be boxcars loaded with lumber. Or there might be plant cars loaded with lumber. But most of the time the good lumber was shipped in boxcars.

speaker: George Lepard
words: Now the big deal to get the logs to the mill from Bovill was to bring the logs down about a 40-mile trip with engines number 21 and 22. And they were very large steam locomotives, quite a bit larger than the ones that carry the passengers. These engines have all been discarded. I really can't tell you where they are except for number one. It has been moved around behind the depot in Potlatch and sets on a separate track and you can see it anytime that you go to Potlatch. It's kind of a curiosity to see the old steam engines. Now getting back to the town of Potlatch, that was… a home town, you might call it a one-man town. All of the real estate, houses, stores, hotels, the school buildings,… and churches were owned by the Potlatch Lumber Company. There was about 300 houses of different designs and they were rented to the people that were working in the mill at a very nominal rate of rent. And it was quite a thriving town. I believe about 1970 or 1930 it would be in the neighborhood of between 1 ,500 and 2 ,000 populations. But I believe today 800 to 1 ,000 would cover it. I mentioned the churches. There was a quite a large following. I remember the first pastor was a Reverend Skates and it wasn't too large a church. It set across the street from grade school and it was used just a very few years when they built a very fine church. It was called Union Church and it burnt down.

speaker: George Lepard
words: They didn't have a church for a while but now they have rebuilt a very nice church that was all built with volunteer labor. The Catholic Church was built and was used all through the years and I believe it's still in use. The Lutheran Church was just a small building, never had very much of a following, but Reverend Anderson that came to Potlatch with the pastor of the Union Church and the last few years I believe the pastor of the Lutheran Church is holding services both at his Lutheran Church and also in the Union Church. I don't know too much about the Catholic Church. I remember Father Pete Cole was one of the first Catholic priests in Potlatch… now… the sawmill itself at the time it was built was considered one of the largest in the United States but that didn't hold good but for a short time because I understand they built another church in the state of Georgia that was larger but not very much. The first engine in the Potlatch mill it was all operated with belts and pulleys and the first engine was 1 ,200 horsepower and 12 boilers provided the steam for that. The first floor of the sawmill was all belts and pulleys. The second floor was where they cut all the lumber… and the third floor was where they brought the bandsaws up to sharpen them and there was also a catwalk for visitors to go through and stand up there and watch the operation in the mill. And there was always someone up there they liked to have the temple come through and see what was going on. The painting mill was a separate machine and band saw for the regular mill and it was run with the same kind of an engine, 20-30 quarter of an engine but it was only 700 horsepower, quite a bit smaller. The last few years these engines were all gone, been dismantled and everything is run with electric motors. And to go through it now and see the difference, in the early days it was all belts and pulleys and there'd be miles of them. Today that is all eliminated.

speaker: Sandie Gittel
words: What's the difference in the amount of manpower used in the mill?

speaker: George Lepard
words: Well the electric motors are cut down on the manpower an awful lot. And the mill alone when I worked in it in 1921, I think it was something like 40 men that took care of the lumber and just the main floor of the sawmill. Today I believe that is cut down to 12. Everything is a push button deal. And you see the father sitting up there pushing buttons where the men used to do the work. He's sitting up high enough that he can see everything that's going on. Now we've mentioned the fact that my father was an early doctor in Idaho. The Potlatch Lumber Company had their own doctors and they were called the company doctors. One of them was a doctor, E .T. Hein, that had a small hospital in Pflug, Washington. And he came up to Potlatch at least twice a week and he had a small office in the building. But the resident doctor was a Dr. Thompson, a very good doctor. He was in Potlatch for many years.

speaker: George Lepard
words: And then when Dr. Hein quit, there was a doctor by the name of Gibson that came from St. Mary's, Idaho. He was a very good surgeon. He was in St. Mary's when the Milwaukee Railroad built through and then he later moved to Bovill. But about 1918 he moved to Potlatch, Idaho. And the first building that they built in Potlatch, they provided two of them for the single men. And they were called the boarding houses, one and two. And in about 1918 they closed up No. 1 boarding house and converted it into a hospital. And Dr. Gibson was the first doctor to take over in the new hospital in Potlatch. And he was there until 1946 when he retired and moved to the coast. And Dr. Thompson retired and moved to Moscow. And for a while they didn't have a doctor there. But at the present time there is a Dr. Biggerstaff in Potlatch and he has been there for about 11 years.

speaker: George Lepard
words: Now in 1934 we moved to Coeur d'Alene. I haven't said where my wife and I met, but we met when I was working in the store in Potlatch, Idaho. Marie Olson was a Coeur d'Alene girl and she came down there as a stenographer. I met her and the only way she could get rid of me was to marry me. We have two boys, one of them sells audio-visual in Spokane. That's to tell you more about what he does, something in the Bell and Howell line. He comes into Coeur d'Alene about every other week and whenever he does, he makes it a point to stop at the junior college to see if they need any of his equipment. Our other boy is graduating from the University of Idaho and he is a civil engineer. And you'll find him in the part and frame, consulting engineer on 4th Street in Coeur d'Alene. George, the oldest boy, graduated from Whitworth College in business.

speaker: Sandie Gittel
words: Your house is on the side of Fort Sherman.

speaker: George Lepard
words: Oh yes, I should dwell on that a little bit. The lot that we live on was bought by my father and all about 1905. He and his brother bought a adjoining lot here at 209 Forest Drive and 211 Forest Drive. 209 Forest Drive. That's where we live and 213 is where the brother lives. And the lot that we were on was originally the band quarters for the band personnel for Fort Sherman. But it burnt up and it was just the empty lot here for a long time. In our alley there's a railroad track between us and the junior college and otherwise our property would, and the street would be adjoining the campus for the junior college. And in the early days there was a single mill just to the south of our property on the lake. And it burnt up about 1898. But I understand that they also saw lumber. And they saw the lumber for the first boat that was built to put on the lake and it was called Amelia Wheaton. And it was named after the youngest daughter of the fourth commander. But I don't want to say too much about Coeur d 'Alene because I didn't come here until 1934. And I think that there are other people who are capable of giving a much better outline than I can.

speaker: George Lepard
words: The, what we call the Little Red Church at the end of the block was the first church for the Fort personnel. And I believe it was for a short time it was also used as a school for the Fort Sherman people. And then there was a nice school built not too far from the Fort, probably about three blocks. It had recently been torn down but that was called the Fort Sherman School. The Fort Sherman School that's here now is a very fine building and it was so close to our home that we could watch our boys go to school from our back door. Now there's one thing about it here. There's a human interest story that comes into this that is really quite different. When I was in Potlatch I went to school with a family and their name was Harris. And they came to Potlatch in 1908 from Chicago, Oregon. And there was the mother and father and three girls and three boys. They were in school with me from I would say about the sixth grade to high school. But one of them, Everett Harris, dropped out of school and was helping his father on a farm and he suddenly disappeared. And they thought that he'd gone up on a small mountain and fell in a mine shaft. Nevertheless they couldn't find him. They even shut down the mill that day to look for him. So everyone gave him up for dead until around 1964 they found out that he was alive. And I think the way they found it out was the fact that he went to Princeton, Idaho.

speaker: Sandie Gittel
words: You were talking about, the Harris family.

speaker: George Lepard
words: Well about 1964 Everett Harris went to Princeton, Idaho, a little town from Potlatch, about three miles from Potlatch. And he inquired as to what had happened to the family. And he was informed they were buried in Chicago, Oregon. So he went down there in the section of the graveyard and gave him the name of Ray Harris in Spokane. And he contacted Ray Harris and sure enough the last few years the remaining members of the family, the two boys and two girls that were left, made it a point to meet with him at least twice a year. Now the reason he wanted to make contact with the family was a friend of his had passed away in California. And she didn't have any heirs and the state of California got the estate. And in the meantime Everett had married and his wife died in 1934. And he had remained in Baker Steel, California where he was manager of the Baker Steel Inn. And he had accumulated a substantial estate and he thought it would be the only thing to contact his brothers and sisters and leave the estate to them because he knew that he was dying of terminal cancer and he wanted to be sure that his family would come into the estate.

speaker: George Lepard
words: After he passed away they had a memorial service in Spokane and all of the friends that they knew were about were notified. And we went into Spokane for the memorial service and it was a very touching thing. There was a lot of the people there that he'd gone to school with and a cousin that was a pastor in a church in California grew up and gave the memorial address and I was very fortunate to be included. Now this last year my wife and I went to Baltimore, Maryland to visit some friends and we went to Washington, D .C. at Gettysburg Battlefield, Harper's Ferry. And the night before we came home we went into a restaurant where they served a specialty of a fish food dish. And our friend said, you ought to order that too. You like fish and I think you have something that you really like. And I did. I had fish food that I'd never heard of. And then when I started to pay for our meal I said, I don't see a cash register around here any place.

speaker: George Lepard
words: Who do you pay? And the father said, well I've been here before and you pay the waitress. I said, okay. So I got up, walked around the table and I walked up to the waitress and I said, you know I was born and raised in the backwoods of northern Idaho and I never ate out very much. And I just didn't know the proper procedure here but I understand I'm to pay you. And the little lady looked up at me and gave me a nice smile and she said, you know a couple years ago my husband and I drove out to Seattle to visit my sister and we stopped at the prettiest little town in northern Idaho and it was called Coeur d 'Alene. And you know it's a small world. And I think with that I'd better quit and wind up.

speaker: Sandie Gittel
words: Have we discussed the school at all in Potlatch?

speaker: George Lepard
words: Well it seems to me that I mentioned the fact that I went to school through the first grade through high school there. But I didn't dwell on it very much. But I might tell you this, that the officials of the warehouse company provided us with a car-papered shack for our first school that stood to the left of where the warehouses down by the railroad track are now. And we only went there one year and they built a real nice school building that was used until just recent years. The school was built up on 6th Street and if I remember correctly there wasn't any furniture in the building and they marched us up and took a picture of the youngsters that were in school in 1907. And in 1908 we went into the new school building. And that was the grade school, first through 8th for many years. And the high school was just a converted Lutheran church that was across the street. The first four graduates of the Potlatch high school graduated from the basement room in the grade school building. And then when they built the new Lutheran church they remodeled the first Lutheran church for a high school building. And that's where I went for four years and I graduated there in 1921. This building was used for the high school for several years. Now they have a new high school to the left of the highway as you come into Potlatch from the Y. And the building that they used for high school for quite a while has been converted to grade school. And the original grade school building has been remodeled and rebuilt and I haven't been in it but it's a very fine apartment house.

speaker: Sandie Gittel
words: Did you know anything about recreation in Potlatch?

speaker: George Lepard
words: Well in the early days there wasn't any recreation in Potlatch. We had good baseball teams. Everybody played baseball and went to the gym. We had a very fine gymnasium and we had quite a lot of activity there. Dances and basketball and indoor baseball which is what we call softball, outdoor softball now. We had indoor baseball. That was about all. There wasn't too much recreation.

speaker: Sandie Gittel
words: Were there any plays?

speaker: George Lepard
words: Yes, we had school plays and it was my very good fortune to be included in quite a lot of them from the time that I was in the seventh grade to high school. I don't remember too much about them but I do remember being in a play that was called Fox and Grandpa that was really a very good comedy. And then the next one that I remember was The Merchant of Venice up to date. And I can remember that because there was a couple of things that were very unusual happened. They, The Merchant of Venice up to date, we had the characters and Portia was looking out of a window up in the stage. I was supposed to whistle and holler and when I did the guy that was going to elope with her hit me across the nose and made my nose bleed. Well, I had on this clown outfit that they rented from an outfit in Spokane and I went over to the edge of the stage and I kept whispering to the hamster and the man that was running the curtain and I kept asking him for a handkerchief. I wasn't talking very loud but I needed a handkerchief off the bed and I wasn't getting it. So finally right in the middle of the whole play I just hollered out, give me a handkerchief. And that brought down the house but I got a handkerchief anyway. And some few days after the play was on they returned the clown outfit to the people in Spokane and they got a bill for $15. Whoever had the clown outfit on ruined it because they got it all covered with blood.

speaker: George Lepard
words: And they questioned me about it and I said, yeah, don't you remember? I asked you for a handkerchief. And that turned out rather funny as well as bad. And I do remember one thing in the play and I'm not too much about it but they wanted to know if they were going elope. And I said, no, they're feeding their musk melon, ... cantaloupe. That's all I remember about it.

speaker: Sandie Gittel
words: Did they have celebrations or anything like that?

speaker: George Lepard
words: Oh yes, they always had a 4th of July celebration and then they had what they called Potlatch Days. And Potlatch Days was a very similar thing that they'd have on the 4th of July. They would have quite a craze, a high school band and a cruise band to join them. And there would be old time machinery, logging equipment and then they'd bring it up to date with the new logging equipment. They don't use the WI&M railroad and flat cars to bring logs from Bovill anymore. The flat cars have all disappeared and they'd bring them in with trucks. So they would show some of the old hard wheel trucks that brought the logs the first time and then they'd show the late modern trucks that they're bringing from Bovill now. The reason for stopping them is to bring them in on trains so they can get into the back country with trucks so much easier than they can on logging trains. And it's quite a weird thing now to see the old logging trucks that the auction would pull around. And I have some very fine pictures of those as well as the old donkey engines that would sit on a skid out in the woods and bring the logs in with tables. And that's gone now. They can just go right into where the logs are with the trucks.

speaker: Sandie Gittel
words: Do you have any interesting hobbies?

speaker: George Lepard
words: Well, I do have a hobby. It's a little bit different than a regular run of the mill, if you want to call it juggling and magic. And I played a little baseball when I was in high school and I started doing a little juggling and then I would quit it, get tired of it. And then I came to Coeur d 'Alene in 1934. I see right away that there was a place for some entertainment so I joined up with a fellow by the name of George Coeur. George Coeur was a barber and he was also a good magician. George and I went around the country and put on a few shows and helped with different programs. And then he left and went to Carson, Washington. So I put in one winner with a fellow by the name of Lee Hoagland in Spokane and we entertained a few high schools. And then I took a couple of tricks from George Coeur and a few from Lee Hoagland and put together my own show, Magic and Juggling. And I'm 74 years old and I helped with the program the first Friday in March. He's come in March.

speaker: Sandie Gittel
words: Pretty good.

speaker: George Lepard
words: I think it's pretty well covered.

speaker: Sandie Gittel
words: Is there anything else about the town you might want to add?

speaker: George Lepard
words: No, I don't think so.

speaker: Sandie Gittel
words: Thank you very much. This tape will be placed in the North Iowa College Library. Thank you for listening.
